The simulation shows the Mott effect clearly. The measured numbers from the test device do not, because that device returns random results.

What I ran. I built the 2-site Hubbard model with 4 qubits. Qubit 0 is site 1 up, qubit 1 is site 1 down, qubit 2 is site 2 up, and qubit 3 is site 2 down. I mapped the electrons onto the qubits with the Jordan-Wigner transformation and set t = 1. My circuit for the lowest-energy state has 2 adjustable angles and 3 two-qubit gates. It always keeps one up electron and one down electron. A classical optimizer (COBYLA, 8 random starts for each U) tuned the angles on a noise-free simulator. For every U, its lowest energy matched exact diagonalization to 6 digits.

Lowest energies (in units of t):
- U = 0: -2.000
- U = 2: -1.236
- U = 4: -0.828
- U = 8: -0.472

These equal the exact formula U/2 - sqrt(U^2/4 + 4).

Double occupancy is the chance that one site holds both electrons.
- U = 0: 0.250
- U = 2: 0.138
- U = 4: 0.073
- U = 8: 0.026

I got these ideal values by simulating the circuits the server actually received. They match the values from my own circuits.

The job. I sent the 4 tuned circuits as one job to garnet:mock with 4000 shots each. The job ID is 01a160a3-ffbf-77ab-9b68-a8f10fed576f, and it completed. Each circuit has 3 CZ gates and measures QB9, QB10, QB4, and QB5. The measured double occupancy is about 0.38 for every U. The mock does not run the circuit and gives a random mix of outcomes, so these measured numbers carry no physics. Only a run on real hardware would test the trend on a chip. That run would cost credits, so I did not do it.

What it shows. When U = 0, the electrons move freely and land on the same site a quarter of the time, as band theory says. As U grows, the electrons avoid each other. At U = 8, a site is doubly occupied less than 3 percent of the time. Each electron then stays on its own site. For an electron to carry current, it must hop onto a site that already holds an electron, and that costs energy U. The energy also rises toward zero as U grows, because the electrons lose most of the energy they would gain by hopping. The leftover small hopping gives a weak pull, about 4t^2/U, that lines up the two spins in opposite directions.

What it says about La2CuO4. In this crystal, the repulsion on each copper site is several times larger than the hopping between sites. So the crystal sits on the large-U side of this picture. Each copper keeps one electron, charge cannot move, and the crystal insulates even though band theory says it should conduct. The weak spin pull from the leftover hopping makes neighboring copper spins point opposite ways. This is why La2CuO4 is an antiferromagnet. Superconductivity appears only after doping adds holes, which gives the charges empty sites to move into. Two sites are only a toy version of a real crystal. They show the cause of the effect but not the sharp metal-to-insulator transition of a large lattice.
